Solution 2 is the only candidate consistent with the Euler characteristic, though I did not independently verify its full homology computation.

**Why Solution 3 fails.** Solution 3 needs a top-degree class in $\widetilde H_{14}(X;\mathbb Q)=H^{BM}_{14}(Y)$. Near a generic point where $Q$ has a real double root, $Y$ is one-sided, so $Y$ is a 14-manifold with nonempty boundary. Such a space has no top Borel–Moore class, so $\widetilde H_{14}=0$ and $t^{14}$ is wrong.

**Why Solution 1 fails.** Because $S$ is a union of open cells $P^\omega\cong\mathbb R^{\dim}$, we have $\chi(X)-1=\chi_c(Y)=\sum_\omega(-1)^{\dim P^\omega}$. Solution 2's cell counts by dimension give $\sum_d(-1)^d\,\#\{\text{cells of dim } d\}=-2$. I checked two of these counts independently: dimension 2 gives 15 and dimension 13 gives 8, both matching my own enumeration. So $\sum_k(-1)^k\dim\widetilde H_k(X;\mathbb Q)=-2$, which rules out the zero answer in Solution 1.

**Why Solution 2 is the consistent one.** Its answer $2t^7$ has Euler characteristic $(-1)^7\cdot 2=-2$, matching the cell count. I have not verified the degree-7 rank of 2 itself, so this is a consistency argument rather than a full proof.

CHOICE: 2
